66.t: Her own politics and why she never voted
66.s: She was drawn into politics through benefits but concluded to stick to music; a clarinet player's voting story put her off voting.
66.ch: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
66.q: Yes, I got hung up in it through working in the Cafe, but I think all musicians or people like me would get mixed up in something, looking for some people to help them and help the race. But they can never be anything but a musician. Through doing benefits and a lot of other things, and you don't…

380.t: Let Freedom Swing and Talbert's NAACP events
380.s: Willard recalls civil rights benefit concerts in the Sixties and Callender cannot recall whether he took part.
380.ch: Tatum, Wiggins and Los Angeles friends
380.q: It seems as though if Eddie Beal and Jimmy Talbert had something to do with it, I would have been there. Because our lives have seemed to criss-cross most of my life, really.

69.s: He opposes independence and says it is dangerous out after eight in San Juan.
69.ch: Band personalities, Duke's last years and the office
69.q: He is Cuban, but now he don't want to, because he's trying to file -- in Puerto Rico, they want to be independent, you know? Some group wants Puerto Rico to be independent, which I don't like, because the first time I hear that Puerto Rico goes independent, I'm going to go downtown and tell them I…

147.t: Musicians' politics, voting and the presidents
147.s: Crawford says the musicians took little interest in politics or voting until Roosevelt, and he praises Truman and Carter.
147.ch: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
147.q: the South, the colored people, they were Republicans. No Democrats around (Inaudible). I just found that out (inaudible).

117.s: Freeman says he never got into politics, citing Trumbo and Casals, and that jazz music is political enough.
117.q: Yes, of course, because as you know, like Dalton Trumbo and of course, John Bright, who wrote Public Enemy, they had to get out of the country, went to Mexico, I guess, and ruined their careers and I think Trumbo died not too long ago.

454.t: Poor whites enslaved by the same people
454.s: Mingus reconsiders blanket anti-white feeling and talks about strikers, miners and Ford.
454.ch: Massey Hall, race and the record business
454.q: See, I really -- I made one mistake in my life, I'm talking about racial prejudice. I always say the white people, well, the white people were enslaved by the same -- the poor white people, the working class, are enslaved by the same people that enslaved the black people.

168.t: Musicians and the civil rights movement
168.s: Musicians sometimes talked about Little Rock and the sit-ins; Stewart says he was too wrapped up in music to think much about it.
168.q: Well, you could hear, once in a while, conversations about that situation, yes. That was more or less a turning point in, what do you call it? Getting together, segregation being -- getting further back in the background, you know, what have you.

77.s: Early interviewers turned out to be Communists panning her government, so she refused to talk to them.
77.q: No. I don't remember. I don't remember anybody. Let me see -- yes, a couple of times some fellows tried to interview me, but I found they were Communists, and I never would talk with them.
